lessons.title: The procession for Athena

n1.text: Six young women walk towards two men. This marble slab comes from the Parthenon in Athens and was carved in the 440s BC.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Look at their hands. Almost every pair is doing something different.

q1.text: Where on the Parthenon was this slab?

correction.truth: The frieze ran high round the outside walls; this slab was on the east side, the front.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Acropolis Museum; the Strasbourg booklet (2022).

b1b.text: Yes. The frieze ran high round the outside of the temple, and this slab was on the east side, the front. Up there it was hard to see.

b1c.text: It was high above people's heads.

correction.tempting: Here it hangs at eye level.
correction.truth: The frieze ran high on the building and was hard to see from below.

n2.text: Every four years, Athens held a great festival for its goddess, Athena. A procession climbed up to the Acropolis.

q2.text: What did the procession bring to Athena?

b2a.text: Yes: the peplos, a robe for Athena's age-old wooden statue. The frieze also shows offerings for a great sacrifice.

correction.tempting: The Parthenon is full of sculpture.
correction.truth: They brought the peplos, a robe for her old wooden statue.
correction.evidence: The Acropolis Museum; the Louvre; Roberts (2025).

correction.truth: The procession carried the peplos, a woven robe for the goddess.
correction.evidence: The Acropolis Museum; the Louvre; Roberts (2025).

n3.text: The slab is named after the Ergastines. Look at the young women on it.

b3a.text: The name means weavers, not carvers.

correction.tempting: The slab is named after them.
correction.truth: The Ergastines were girls who wove Athena's robe.

correction.tempting: They walk in a religious procession.
correction.truth: The Ergastines were girls who wove the robe; the two men are the ones sometimes called priests.

b3c.text: Yes. They wove Athena's peplos. Whether these women are Ergastines or basket-bearers, scholars disagree.

n4.text: In 1789 Fauvel recovered this slab from the Parthenon ruins, working for the French ambassador Choiseul-Gouffier. The whole frieze had been about 160 metres long.

voice.speaker: guide
voice.text: Somebody planned all 160 metres. Scholars give that person a name.

q4.text: Who is credited with designing the frieze?

b4a.text: He recovered the slab, much later.

correction.tempting: His name is in the slab's history.
correction.truth: Fauvel recovered it from the ruins in 1789. The design is attributed to Phidias.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Strasbourg booklet (2022); Rémond (2021); Roberts (2025).

b4b.text: Yes. The Louvre and scholars such as Roberts attribute the frieze's design to Phidias. It is an attribution, made by scholars.

b4c.text: He owned the slab, centuries later.

correction.tempting: His name is in the slab's history.
correction.truth: He was the French ambassador it was recovered for in 1789. The design is attributed to Phidias.

n5.text: From the ruins in Athens, the slab still had a long way to go before it reached the Louvre.

q5.text: How did the slab reach the Louvre?

b5a.text: It was seized on land, by the state.

correction.tempting: Marble from Greece had to cross the sea.
correction.truth: It was seized by the revolutionary authorities with Choiseul-Gouffier's collections, and entered the Louvre in 1798.
It was seized in the Revolution and entered the Louvre in 1798.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; the Strasbourg booklet (2022); Rémond (2021).

b5c.text: Yes. Choiseul-Gouffier's collections were confiscated in the French Revolution, and the slab entered the Louvre in 1798.

n6.text: It has been in Paris since 1798, now in Room 347 on Floor 0 of the Denon wing. Other slabs of the same frieze are in Athens and London.

lessons.takeaway: This slab once ran high on the front of the Parthenon, showing young women in the procession that brought a woven robe to Athena; it reached Paris through a revolutionary seizure.
